newsitem.title: UK: British MPs expect modest tax cuts from prudent Clarke.
newsitem.headline: British MPs expect modest tax cuts from prudent Clarke.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke is likely to resist political pressure for deep tax cuts and deliver a prudent budget next week, according to members of parliament's Treasury Select Committee.

Reflecting the consensus in financial and political circles, they said the strength of Britain's consumer-led recovery and the need to keep government borrowing down would limit Clarke's scope for give-aways in the run-up to the general election.
But they said they expected Clarke to find enough savings to cut the standard income tax rate to 23 percent from 24 percent.
Members of the committee also said they expected Clarke to clamp down on tax relief on profit-related pay, which costs the Treasury some 1.5 billion pounds ($2.5 billion) a year.

Matthew Carrington, the Conservative chairman of the panel, estimated Clarke would have 3-5 billion pounds to "give away" from a combination of fiscal drag -- the tendency for tax receipts to rise over time -- and spending cuts.

"It's a penny off income tax, plus indexing. I'd expect him to index all the thresholds," Carrington said, adding that the quarter-point interest rate rise to six percent Clarke ordered on October 30 meant he could be a bit more relaxed on taxes.
"But what the interest rate rise shows is that his budget is going to be a cautious budget. It's not going to be an electioneering budget," Carrington predicted.
This view was shared by fellow Conservative Quentin Davies.

"He will not -- as he has not in the previous two years -- give in to any kind of pressure to do anything irresponsible on ther fiscal front. We will continue our progress in reducing the public sector borrowing requirement," Davies said.

Not surprisingly, opposition MPs were not convinced that the politically astute Clarke would put country before party, which trails Labour in opinion polls by about 20 percentage points with the election six months away at most.

"It's not clear to what extent he's just going to go for broke in a last-minute bid to save the election," Labour MP Stephen Timms said. "What he will do seems to me to be entirely a party-political consideration."
Another Labour MP, Ian Pearson, saw a 50 percent chance of a one-percent cut in standard income tax plus a widening of the income band on which tax is paid at the rate of just 20 percent.

He thought Clarke was unlikely to pander to Conservatives in marginal constituencies who are clamouring for a vote-grabbing tax cut of two pence in the pound. To do so would damage his reputation as chancellor and thus his leadership prospects.

"I think that would be extremely dangerous indeed for the economy. I think it would go down incredibly badly in the markets and Clarke would blow any credibility that he has as a prudent chancellor if he did it," Pearson said.

Malcolm Bruce of the Liberal Democrats also said he suspected Clarke might go for the moral high ground by offering little in the way of net tax cuts in order to keep a lid on interest rates in the run-up to the election.
Bruce admitted the political pressures on Clarke to cut the basic rate of tax are enormous.
